summary: Specifies the rules for deciding whether a Unicode code point, alone or in its context, may be used in an internationalized domain name. It is part of the IDNA2008 specification. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Not every letter or symbol is allowed in a website name. This is the rulebook saying which characters can be used and when.

subtitle: The rulebook that decides which Unicode characters may appear in an internationalized domain name.

tldr.problem: Domain names need to carry characters from many scripts, but not every Unicode code point is safe or useful in a name. Older approaches excluded a small list of bad characters instead of naming the good ones.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5892 sorts every code point into overlapping categories based on Unicode properties and a short exceptions list. A fixed procedure then gives each code point one of five values: PVALID, CONTEXTJ, CONTEXTO, DISALLOWED or UNASSIGNED.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard in the IDNA2008 series, and RFC 8753 updates it. Because it defines a procedure rather than a table, it works for new Unicode versions too.

today: RFC 5892 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8753. It remains part of the IDNA2008 document set alongside RFC 5890, RFC 5891, RFC 5893 and RFC 5894.

sections.title: Why an Inclusion-Based Rule
sections.content:
RFC 5892 is one document in the IDNA2008 (Internationalizing Domain Names in Applications) series. It specifies rules for deciding whether a code point, on its own or in context, is a candidate for inclusion in an Internationalized Domain Name (IDN).

It follows advice from RFC 4690, which says that lists of code points should be built by naming the characters that are permitted. Stringprep (RFC 3454) and Nameprep (RFC 3491) did the opposite: they excluded a small number of characters from the whole Unicode set.

This RFC does not say how the values are applied to a label. That belongs to the protocol document, RFC 5891. The RFC is explicit that a value for one character is not enough to decide whether a whole label is usable, because some combinations are inadvisable under script-specific rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a guest list for a party. Instead of listing everyone who is banned, this rulebook lists the guests who are allowed in, which is much safer.

sections.title: The Five Property Values
sections.content:
Every code point ends up with one value of a derived property:

  • PVALID (protocol valid): allowed for general use in IDNs. A label made only of these is still not automatically usable in the DNS.
  • CONTEXTJ and CONTEXTO: a contextual rule is required. CONTEXTJ is for Join_Control characters and CONTEXTO is for other characters. Such a character must not be used unless a suitable rule exists and the context satisfies it.
  • DISALLOWED: should clearly not be in IDNs.
  • UNASSIGNED: not designated in the Unicode Standard.

For the two Join Control characters, U+200D ZERO WIDTH JOINER and U+200C ZERO WIDTH NON-JOINER, the value is CONTEXTJ. The RFC says it is invalid to register a string containing a contextual character, or even to look one up, unless the rule is found and satisfied.
sections.plainLanguage: Some characters are always welcome, some are never welcome, and a few are welcome only if standing next to the right friends.

sections.title: The Ten Categories
sections.content:
The derived value comes from a two-step procedure. First, each code point is placed in one or more categories, based on Unicode properties or on its own code point value. The categories are not mutually exclusive. Second, set operations over those categories pick the final value.

The categories are labelled A to J:

  • A, LetterDigits: General_Category is Ll, Lu, Lo, Nd, Lm, Mn or Mc. These are the characters commonly used in mnemonics.
  • B, Unstable: toNFKC(toCaseFold(toNFKC(cp))) != cp, meaning the code point changes under case folding and NFKC normalization.
  • C, IgnorableProperties: default-ignorable, white space or noncharacter code points.
  • D, IgnorableBlocks: Combining Diacritical Marks for Symbols, Musical Symbols and Ancient Greek Musical Notation.
  • E, LDH: 002D, 0030..0039 and 0061..007A, the traditional hostname characters (hyphen, digits and a to z).
  • F, Exceptions: an explicit list of code points that the Unicode properties alone cannot classify correctly.
  • G, BackwardCompatible: a set that is empty in this RFC and exists so the results can be kept stable if Unicode properties change later.
  • H, JoinControl: characters with Join_Control true.
  • I, OldHangulJamo: conjoining Hangul Jamo (Leading, Vowel and Trailing). Excluding them limits Korean to preformed, modern Hangul syllables.
  • J, Unassigned: General_Category Cn, excluding noncharacters.
sections.plainLanguage: Characters get sorted into ten buckets, such as letters, invisible characters, odd music symbols and special cases. The bucket a character falls into helps decide whether it can be used.

sections.title: Calculating the Derived Property
sections.content:
The algorithm is a single ordered list of checks. The first rule that matches decides the value. Exceptions come first, so an explicit entry always wins. Then BackwardCompatible and Unassigned are checked. After that, LDH gives PVALID and JoinControl gives CONTEXTJ. Next come the exclusion categories (Unstable, IgnorableProperties, IgnorableBlocks and OldHangulJamo), all giving DISALLOWED. Only then does LetterDigits give PVALID. Anything left over is DISALLOWED.

The Exceptions table has three kinds of entries. Some code points would otherwise be DISALLOWED but are PVALID (for example 00DF LATIN SMALL LETTER SHARP S and 03C2 GREEK SMALL LETTER FINAL SIGMA). Some would otherwise be DISALLOWED but are CONTEXTO (for example 00B7 MIDDLE DOT). The Arabic-Indic and Extended Arabic-Indic digits would otherwise be PVALID but are CONTEXTO. Some, such as 0640 ARABIC TATWEEL, would otherwise be PVALID but are DISALLOWED.

Sections 2 and 3 are normative. The huge table in Appendix B, which applies the rules to code points 0x0000 to 0x10FFFF for Unicode 5.2, is non-normative and for illustration only.
sections.plainLanguage: It works like a sorting checklist at a door. The guard goes down the list in order, and the first rule that fits decides whether you get in, need a helper, or are turned away.

sections.title: Contextual Rules
sections.content:
Appendix A defines the rules for characters that need context. They are written in a small pseudo-code in which each rule is a Boolean expression, and a special value Undefined covers errors such as looking before the first character of a label. Before and After refer to network order in the label, not the visual display order, which may be reversed for right-to-left scripts.

Nine rules are given:

  • U+200C ZERO WIDTH NON-JOINER: allowed after a virama, or inside a defined joining pattern in cursive scripts such as Arabic.
  • U+200D ZERO WIDTH JOINER: allowed only right after a virama.
  • U+00B7 MIDDLE DOT: only between two l (U+006C) characters, which permits the Catalan ela geminada.
  • U+0375 GREEK LOWER NUMERAL SIGN: the following character must be Greek.
  • U+05F3 and U+05F4 (Hebrew geresh and gershayim): the preceding character must be Hebrew.
  • U+30FB KATAKANA MIDDLE DOT: the label must contain at least one Hiragana, Katakana or Han character.
  • Arabic-Indic digits (0660..0669) and Extended Arabic-Indic digits (06F0..06F9): the two sets cannot be mixed in one label.

Each rule has a Lookup field. It is True for the two joiner rules, meaning application at lookup time is recommended, and False for the others.
sections.plainLanguage: A few characters are like shy guests who only come if the right friend is next to them. The rules check that the right friend is there before letting them in.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA created an IDNA-Derived Property Value registry covering Unicode 5.2 and later versions. Its values are calculated together with a designated expert by following Sections 2 and 3, not by copying the non-normative Appendix B table. Problems are flagged for the IESG. Changes to the rules, including the BackwardCompatible set, require IETF Review as described in RFC 5226.

A second registry, the IDNA Context Registry, holds the approved contextual rules for CONTEXTO and CONTEXTJ characters. Additions or changes also need IETF Review. A new rule is described by a template with the fields Name, Code point, Overview, Lookup and Rule Set.
sections.plainLanguage: The official lists are kept in a public notebook run by IANA, and changing a rule needs a proper review first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This RFC keeps its security section short and points elsewhere. Security considerations for this version of IDNA are described in the Definitions document, RFC 5890. Specific issues for labels with scripts written right to left appear in the Bidi document, RFC 5893.
sections.plainLanguage: This rulebook says the safety advice is written in two other books and tells you where to find them.
